raw_case_text: In February 2016, a male in his 40s was admitted to the neurology department of a hospital in Paramaribo, Suriname, because of muscle weakness in the legs, which started 7 days prior to admission. At presentation in the hospital, the patient was unable to walk without help. Two weeks before muscle weakness started he visited the hospital because of urinary retention. Acute myelitis and a cauda syndrome were excluded with an MRI-scan, which showed no abnormalities. The week before muscle weakness started he had an influenza-like syndrome and had a short episode of diplopia. At first physical examination after admission, muscle weakness was observed in predominantly the legs (MRC score 4). Areflexia in both legs and arms was noted. The patient complained of paresthesias and pain in the legs but did not have a sensory level or other signs of myelum involvement. A lumbar puncture was performed 2 days after admission, and a high protein level was found in the CSF (4.4 g/L) while the cell count was slightly increased (32.7 x 106/L). A urine sample, taken at day two after admission, was tested positive for ZIKV RNA with a Ct-value of 35.7. Four days after admission his muscle power improved (MCR score arms 5, legs; proximal 5, distal 4), while the areflexia in arms and legs persisted. Because of the little availability of IVIg in Suriname and because PE is not possible in Suriname, the patient did not received immunotherapy. A motor NCS, performed 15 days after the start of muscle weakness, showed severe decreased NCV and a prolonged DML in all tested nerves. The CMAP was decreased in predominantly the legs (see Table S2 in Supplementary Material). These results were consistent with the demyelinating subtype of GBS. At discharge, 7 days after admission, he was still unable to walk without help due to muscle weakness in the legs. Four months after hospital discharge he was able to walk a few steps without assistance, but he still could not live independently or return to work.

subjective.chief_complaint: A man in his forties presented in February 2016 with a 7-day history of progressive lower extremity muscle weakness rendering him unable to walk unassisted.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: In February 2016, the patient was admitted to the neurology department in Paramaribo, Suriname, with a 7-day history of progressive leg weakness, paresthesias, and leg pain, leaving him unable to walk without assistance. Two weeks before the onset of weakness, he had presented to the hospital with urinary retention (at which time a spinal MRI was normal). One week prior to weakness onset, he experienced an influenza-like illness accompanied by a brief episode of diplopia.
subjective.past_medical_history: Resident of Paramaribo, Suriname; history of urinary retention 2 weeks prior to neurologic onset.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for leg weakness, leg pain, paresthesias, preceding urinary retention, influenza-like symptoms, and transient diplopia.

objective.physical_examination: Initial neurological examination showed symmetrical muscle weakness predominantly affecting the lower limbs (MRC score 4/5) and global areflexia in both upper and lower extremities, with no sensory level or signs of myelopathy, and inability to ambulate without assistance.
objective.advanced_workup: Prior spinal MRI performed for urinary retention showed no abnormalities, excluding acute myelitis and cauda equina syndrome. Lumbar puncture on hospital day 2 demonstrated markedly elevated CSF protein of 4.4 g/L with a mildly increased CSF cell count of 32.7 x 10^6/L. Motor nerve conduction studies (NCS) performed 15 days after weakness onset revealed severely decreased nerve conduction velocities (NCV), prolonged distal motor latencies (DML) in all tested nerves, and reduced compound muscle action potentials (CMAP) predominantly in the lower limbs, consistent with the demyelinating subtype of Guillain-Barre syndrome.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Zika virus-associated demyelinating Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS), confirmed by positive urine ZIKV real-time RT-PCR on hospital day 2 (Ct value 35.7). Due to limited availability of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) and lack of plasma exchange (PE) facilities in Suriname, the patient did not receive immunotherapy. By hospital day 4, his muscle strength partially improved (MRC 5/5 in arms, 5/5 in proximal legs, 4/5 in distal legs) with persistent four-limb areflexia. He was discharged on hospital day 7 still unable to walk unassisted; at 4 months post-discharge, he could walk a few steps independently but remained unable to live independently or return to work.
